key_facts: **Inherited** skin fragility: blisters after **minimal trauma** due to defective adhesion proteins.
Types by split level: **EB simplex** (keratins 5/14, intraepidermal), **junctional** (laminin-332, lamina lucida), **dystrophic** (type VII collagen, below lamina densa, scarring), **Kindler**.
Differs from **EB acquisita**, an autoimmune adult disease.
Refer urgently any baby with unexplained blistering to the EB team.
Handle gently: no adhesive tapes, lift on a soft pad, silicone dressings; don't lance blisters unless trained.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: A group of **inherited mechanobullous disorders**: skin (and often mucosa) blisters after **minimal trauma**, because adhesion molecules are defective. This is different from **EB acquisita**, which is autoimmune and usually affects adults.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors

fig.caption: Skin fragility in EB: the level of the split in EB simplex, junctional and dystrophic EB compared with normal skin.

blocks: Loss of structural integrity at a specific skin level means minor shear causes a blister. Inheritance is autosomal dominant or recessive depending on subtype. **Key Module 6 links: DEB is caused by type VII collagen (COL7A1) defects, and chronic RDEB wounds carry a high risk of cutaneous SCC.**

ul: **"EB is contagious"**: it is genetic.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: The **level of the missing glue** decides EB type and severity.

mech.t: Laminin-332 or integrin loss separates epidermis from basement membrane.
Type VII collagen loss splits the skin beneath the basement membrane, healing with scars and milia.
mech.caption: EB types split at different levels: within the basal cells, in the basement membrane, or beneath it.

ul: Blisters and erosions at **friction sites** (hands, feet, belt line, nappy area). They may be present at birth.
Nail dystrophy, milia and scarring (especially dystrophic types). Mitten deformities in severe RDEB.
**Mucosa:** mouth, oesophagus (dysphagia), larynx (hoarse cry in severe JEB).
Localised EBS often presents when the child starts **crawling or walking**.
A neonate with unexplained blistering, with or without congenital absence of skin: **consider EB until proven otherwise**.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Urgent recognition and referral to a **specialist EB centre** (UK: e.g. GOSH and other DEBRA-linked centres). Subtyping uses immunofluorescence mapping, electron microscopy and genetic testing. Primary care does **not** attempt to subtype.

ddx.name: Friction or sucking blisters
ddx.f: Localised; well baby; no family history

blocks.title: A specialist multidisciplinary disease
blocks.text: The IP and pharmacist role is recognition, safe interim handling, timely referral, and medicines support under the EB team’s plan.

ul: **Refer urgently** any baby with unexplained fragility or blistering to paediatric dermatology or the EB team. For GOSH, contact the dermatology registrar via switchboard.
**Handle gently:** no adhesive tapes, lift on a soft pad rather than under the arms, keep the environment cool, and reduce friction.
Do **not** lance blisters unless trained in EB technique. Specialist nurses teach sterile piercing and silicone dressings.
**Dressings:** soft silicone or low-adherent, with no ordinary adhesives. Emollients and paraffin to lubricate.
Pain, constipation, nutrition, dental and eye care through the MDT.
Infection: colonisation is common. Discuss significant infection with the EB team.
**Medicines optimisation:** liquid formulations if there are oesophageal strictures, avoid rectal routes where possible, and check interactions.
Awareness: **Oleogel-S10** (birch triterpenes) is a specialist wound therapy for selected JEB and DEB wounds.
**RDEB:** surveillance for **SCC**. Any changing chronic wound needs urgent dermatology review.

refer.t: Respiratory distress or hoarseness (airway involvement in JEB).
Dehydration, failure to thrive, or sepsis.
A new, enlarging or ulcerating chronic wound in RDEB (**SCC**).

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Respiratory distress or hoarseness (airway involvement in JEB).
Dehydration, failure to thrive, or sepsis.
A new, enlarging or ulcerating chronic wound in RDEB (**SCC**).
Infection, malnutrition, anaemia, strictures, fusion of fingers (DEB), aggressive SCC (recessive DEB).
EBS often improves with age; severe JEB and recessive DEB are life-limiting.

pearls: Give parents **DEBRA UK** support details early.
Genetic counselling for future pregnancies is a specialist role.
Never blame ‘rough handling’ alone when true fragility is present.
Even mild localised EBS benefits from a correct diagnosis (footwear and blister care education).

quiz.q: When should you think of Epidermolysis bullosa (EB)?
quiz.a: A neonate or infant with blisters and erosions from minimal friction (hands, feet, nappy area), ± absent skin at birth, nail dystrophy or mouth blisters.
Inherited defects in adhesion proteins; the level of split defines the type (simplex, junctional, dystrophic, Kindler).

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Urgent referral to an EB centre, gentle handling, no adhesives, and soft silicone dressings under specialist guidance.
Airway involvement (hoarse cry in JEB), sepsis, dehydration or failure to thrive, and SCC in chronic RDEB wounds.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Respiratory distress or hoarseness (airway involvement in JEB).
